sections.h2: What happens to a tenant when a North Carolina landlord sells the rental?
sections.html:
The tenant's deposit travels with the sale. When a landlord's interest ends by sale, assignment, death or a receiver's appointment, G.S. 42-54 starts a 30-day clock.

The seller has two choices. One is to pass the unspent deposit to the buyer and mail the tenant a notice naming the buyer and giving an address. The other is to refund the tenant directly. Either choice ends the seller's liability for that money. A buyer inheriting tenants should leave closing with the deposit ledger, the leases and any written repair requests.

sections.h2: How much security deposit can a North Carolina landlord hold?
sections.html:
The cap scales with the tenancy. Section 42-51(b) allows two weeks' rent on a weekly tenancy, a month and a half of rent on a monthly one, and two months' rent on any longer term.

  • Deposits may cover unpaid rent and certain water, sewer or electric charges.
  • They may cover damage to the unit, including damaged smoke or carbon monoxide alarms.
  • They may cover re-renting costs after a breach, including a broker's reasonable fee.
  • They may cover removal and storage of belongings after a summary ejectment case, plus court costs.

The landlord owes the tenant a written, itemized accounting within a month of the tenancy ending and the keys coming back. A claim that is still unsettled then requires an interim report at that point and a final one by day 60. Ordinary wear and tear is off limits, and the amount kept cannot exceed real damages.

sections.h2: What repairs must a North Carolina landlord make?
sections.html:
A landlord has to keep the home fit and habitable, and G.S. 42-42(a) lists the duties. They include complying with building and housing codes, keeping common areas safe, and maintaining electrical, plumbing, heating and cooling systems, with prompt repair after the tenant gives written notice except in emergencies.

The statute also requires working smoke alarms, replaced or repaired within fifteen days after the tenant writes to the landlord, and at least one carbon monoxide alarm per level in units with a fuel-burning heater, appliance or fireplace, or an attached garage. When a landlord installs or replaces a smoke alarm, the statute calls for a tamper-resistant 10-year lithium battery model unless the unit has a hardwired alarm with battery backup or a combined smoke and carbon monoxide alarm. Imminently dangerous conditions must be fixed within a reasonable time. The list includes unsafe wiring or steps, no potable water, no operable toilet and, from November 1 through March 31, no heating that can reach 65 degrees when it is 20 degrees outside.

A tenant cannot waive these duties by accepting a bad unit. A seller should therefore treat open code or alarm problems as part of what the buyer receives, and ask the county inspections office what is on file.

sections.h2: Can a North Carolina landlord evict a tenant for asking for repairs?
sections.html:
No, not in retaliation. G.S. 42-37.1 protects good-faith repair requests, complaints to a government agency, a formal complaint by a government authority, efforts to enforce lease or legal rights, and joining a tenants' organization.

In a summary ejectment case, a tenant can raise retaliation as a defense by showing that the landlord's action substantially responds to one of those acts within 12 months before filing. The landlord can still prevail in several situations: the tenant breached the rent covenant or another substantial lease term, a fixed term ended without a renewal option, the tenant primarily caused the violation, code compliance requires emptying the unit, an earlier good-faith notice to quit was already delivered, or the owner sincerely wants the home to live in, plans a remodel that displaces the household, or will take it off the rental market for six months or longer.

sections.h2: What notice ends each type of North Carolina tenancy?
sections.html:
Source: G.S. 42-14, 42-3 and 42-26
SituationNotice or step
Yearly leaseA month or more before the year runs out
Monthly leaseSeven days
Weekly leaseTwo days
Manufactured home lot60 days or more ahead of the period's end
Unpaid rentTerm forfeited when past-due rent stays unpaid 10 days after a demand

Summary ejectment under G.S. 42-26 covers holding over after the term, breaching a condition that ends the estate, and desertion while in arrears. Back charges for water, sewer or electric service do not justify ending a lease.

sections.h2: How does a North Carolina eviction case move through court?
sections.html:
The landlord files in small claims before a magistrate. Court dates land within a month of filing, and eviction cases often get one in 10 to 15 days. The court system prints a $96 filing fee and a $30 sheriff service fee, and there is no jury in small claims.

  • A defendant served fewer than two days before the hearing is entitled to a continuance.
  • Either side can take the case to district court, orally in the courtroom or in writing, inside a ten-day window after the magistrate rules.
  • Appeal costs must be paid, and a bond may be required to stop enforcement.

An owner who wants the house empty should plan around that timeline. Changing locks or removing belongings without a court order is not a shortcut, because eviction here runs through the court and the sheriff.

sections.h2: What happens to tenants when a North Carolina lender forecloses?
sections.html:
Tenants of a foreclosed rental get some breathing room. A notice of sale for a residential building of under fifteen rental units must say that an order for possession may issue, and a tenant whose lease was signed or renewed from October 1, 2007 forward may end it on notice of 10 to 90 days measured from the sale date.

After a sale is reported, anyone can submit an upset bid within 10 days if it exceeds the last bid by at least 5% and at least $750, and each upset bid restarts a 10-day period. Each upset bid also pushes the final date back, so tenants should watch the court file for the confirmed sale.

sections.h2: What should a seller of a North Carolina rental do before listing?
sections.html:
Begin with the lease file. Record each tenant's term, the deposit held and the date a notice to quit could take effect, then choose between a sale with occupants or an empty house.

If tenants stay, hand the buyer the deposit records so the 30-day transfer duty is met. If the unit will be empty, work through the notice periods and the court process, and give a monthly tenant at least the seven days the statute requires. Have a local attorney look over the plan if a repair complaint is open, since a retaliation defense can slow a case.

faqs.q: When must a North Carolina landlord return a security deposit?
faqs.a: By mail or hand delivery, with an itemized damage list and the balance, no later than 30 days after the tenancy ends and possession returns. An unsettled claim needs an interim accounting by then and a final one by day 60.

faqs.q: How high can a North Carolina deposit go?
faqs.a: Two weeks' rent on a weekly tenancy, one and a half months' on a monthly one, and two months' on longer terms.

faqs.q: How much warning does a monthly tenant in North Carolina get?
faqs.a: Seven days. Weekly tenancies need two days, and yearly ones a month or more before the year ends.

faqs.q: Who holds the deposit after a North Carolina landlord sells?
faqs.a: Within 30 days the seller must either pass it to the new owner and notify the tenant by mail, or refund it to the tenant.

faqs.q: Can a North Carolina tenant stay after a foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: For a while. Sale notices for small residential rentals must warn that a possession order may issue, and tenants under qualifying leases may end the lease on 10 to 90 days' notice after the sale date.
